## Korean Food

Korean restaurants were starting to take off in a big way just before the pandemic, providing a novel alternative to more familiar Asian cuisines. But public health closures and the economic fallout hit them particularly hard. As people cut their spending and reverted to the comfortingly familiar, the number of restaurants [dropped from over 7,500 to 6,700](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1178889/number-of-korean-restaurant-industry-businesses-us/).

A few years later, things are turning around. There was a [10% growth in locations](https://www.circana.com/intelligence/press-releases/2024/south-korean-restaurant-locations-in-the-u-s-grow-10-over-the-past-year-amid-surge-in-demand-for-korean-cuisine/) in the year to September 2024, with larger numbers of both full and quick service restaurants. This is tied into a wider wave of interest in Korean culture, as K-pop and K-dramas take America by storm. Korean sauces, kimchi, and dalgona coffee have all found their fans, while a wider pool of consumers is becoming curious about these novelties.

[36% of Korean restaurants](https://www.circana.com/intelligence/press-releases/2024/south-korean-restaurant-locations-in-the-u-s-grow-10-over-the-past-year-amid-surge-in-demand-for-korean-cuisine/) are concentrated in key markets, leaving many market areas untouched, so there are plenty of territories with no Korean restaurant competition.

## Indian Food

Though Indians make up the second-largest community of Asian Americans, they’ve historically had a relatively small impact on the nation’s cuisine. Indian immigrants are proportionally more likely to be highly skilled professionals taking on specialist jobs, so they haven’t taken up less prestigious jobs such as cooking.

But the rising income and influence of Indian Americans has got this cuisine moving. There are now over [4,100 Indian restaurants in the US](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/indian-restaurants-industry/), ranging from fast casual to fine dining. Indian restaurants were worth $4.9 billion in 2024, after growing by an [average of 2.1% per year](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/indian-restaurants-industry/) for the previous five years.

Though Indian food is sometimes served to take out, [three-quarters of sales](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/indian-restaurants-industry/) are for consumption on the premises. As with Chinese food, many people come to enjoy the dining experience.

[Indo-Chinese cuisine](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-67411824), a fusion that’s popular in India, is also on the rise, providing an extra novelty for those wanting something new. And as the waves of different styles spreading through the Asian restaurant market show, Americans remain ready to keep trying new things.

## The Top Asian Restaurant Franchises of 2026

### 1. Panda Express

[Panda Express](https://www.pandaexpress.com/licensing-opportunities) is a chain of American Chinese restaurants, but the standalone restaurants are company-owned and not franchised. The company does license its brand to non-traditional venues such as airports, universities, military bases, hospitals, casinos, amusement parks, and stadiums. The menu of China-inspired fare is extensive but varies by location.

Founded by Andrew and Peggy Cherng in Glendale, California, in 1983, the company website claims there are more than 2,600 locations (it opened its 2,000th store in 2020), most of which are in the US but also in a variety of other countries (Canada, South Korea, Mexico, United Arab Emirates, Japan, El Salvador, Aruba, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Guatemala, and the Philippines).

### 2. L&L Hawaiian Barbecue

[L&L Hawaiian Barbecue](https://www.hawaiianbarbecue.com/franchise/) offers a mash-up menu of influences, including Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, American, and Korean dishes served in the form of the traditional Hawaiian barbecue plate lunch with two scoops of rice, a creamy macaroni salad, and a hot entrée. There’s even Spam on the menu with Spam Musubi – a slice of grilled spam on rice wrapped in dry seaweed – and Spam Saimin (a noodle soup with Spam and fresh green onions).

Founded by Johnson Kam and Eddie Flores Jr. in Honolulu, Hawaii, in 1976 and franchising since 1991, the number of locations currently stands at 231 (up from the previously reported total of 227), of which seven are company-owned and two are located outside the US.

### 3. Teriyaki Madness

[Teriyaki Madness](https://franchise.teriyakimadness.com/) is a fast-casual Asian concept featuring a menu of nine signature bowls (various chicken, beef, and tofu combinations), four appetizers, five side dishes, and seven different house-made sauces. The company has also been testing a mobile food truck concept that may become a franchisee option.

Founded in 2003 and franchising since 2005, the number of locations has risen rapidly in recent years from 15 in 2014 to the current total of 202 (up from the previously reported total of 187), of which one is company-owned and one is located outside the US.

### 4. WaBa Grill

[WaBa Grill](https://wabagrillfranchising.com/) is a chain of rice-bowl restaurants with a relatively simple menu that includes sweet and spicy chicken bowls and plates, in-house marinated rib-eye steak bowls and plates, Waba (chicken and steak) bowls and plates, plant-based steak bowls and plates, wild-caught salmon bowls and plates, shrimp bowls and plates, and tofu bowls and plates. Other items on the menu include Boom Boom Tacos, salads, sides/appetizers, and four sauces.

Founded in 2004 and franchising since 2006, the number of locations has expanded in recent years from 162 in 2017 to the current total of 193 (up from the previously reported total of 191), of which five are company-owned and all are located in the US.

### 5. Jinya Ramen Bar

[Jinya Ramen Bar](https://www.jinyaramenbar.com/franchise/) presents a menu of the perennial favorite Japanese dish known as ramen, but this is not your average instant ramen. The broths are slow-simmered for more than 20 hours, balancing flavors from whole pork bones, chicken, and vegetables with bonito, dashi, miso, kombu, and other classic Japanese ingredients. The result is a rich broth that is thick and full-flavored. On the menu are more than a dozen signature ramen bowls, a dozen different “small plates” (appetizers), mini tacos, salads, curried rice bowls, and desserts.

Founded by Tomo Takahashi in California in 2010 and franchising since 2012, there are now 78 locations (up from the previously reported total of 63), of which five are company-owned and six are located outside the US.

Mexican-style cooking has brought a host of techniques and flavors to the American dining table. And as the popularity of Mexican food continues to grow, the same is happening for Mexican restaurant franchises.

## A National Favorite

While it’s often talked about as something in its own niche, Mexican food has become mainstream fair in American dining. A 2020 survey showed that [over 238 million Americans](https://www.statista.com/statistics/281028/us-households-consumption-of-mexican-food-and-ingredients/) consumed Mexican food or ingredients, while fewer than 92 million didn’t. Tortillas have become the [second most popular type of bread in the country](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/mexican-restaurants-industry/#IndustryStatisticsAndTrends/), second only to white bread, and chimichangas are the signature food of one of the most popular superheroes in Hollywood, even though Deadpool himself has no Mexican connections.

The cultural power of Mexican food extends to restaurants. Mexican is third only to American and Italian style cuisine as the most popular dining option in the country, and it’s common for restaurants with varied menus to include Mexican options. [Even other Hispanic restaurants quite often serve Mexican food](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/01/11/about-1-in-10-restaurants-in-the-us-serve-mexican-food/), while Mexican restaurants seldom return the favor.

Of course, this is also good news for the restaurants specifically serving Mexican food. There are [nearly 50,000 Mexican restaurants](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/mexican-restaurants-industry/#IndustryStatisticsAndTrends/) across the US, [employing 963,000 staff](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/mexican-restaurants-industry/#IndustryStatisticsAndTrends/). Around [one in ten restaurants](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/01/11/about-1-in-10-restaurants-in-the-us-serve-mexican-food/) in the US now serves Mexican food, and the more restaurants there are, the more people get used to this cuisine.

While a lot of this is driven by the wider population’s adoption of Mexican food, immigration is a factor. Hispanic immigrants provide both demand and supply for Mexican cooking, which dominates the Hispanic restaurant scene. While there are other types of Hispanic restaurants, [none of them makes up more than 1% of the restaurant market](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/01/11/about-1-in-10-restaurants-in-the-us-serve-mexican-food/). Mexican food has become the iconic taste of the south.

The development of fusions and variations such as Tex-Mex has further fueled growth. They make it easier for people to try Mexican alongside something else, or to incorporate a Mexican touch into a more familiar meal. Cross-cultural restaurants also add novelty and variety to the dining experience, refreshing people’s interest.

Franchising is common in this sector, with major chains using it to quickly expand and tap into growing demand. Some big-name franchises are based in this sector, offering opportunities for new franchisees.

## The Economics of Mexican Restaurant Franchising

The Mexican restaurant industry had [$96.4 billion in revenues in 2024](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/mexican-restaurants-industry/#IndustryStatisticsAndTrends/), having [grown by an average of 4.7% per year](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/mexican-restaurants-industry/#IndustryStatisticsAndTrends/) for the previous five years. That ongoing growth makes it a promising sector for those looking to get into franchising.

The serving style of Mexican restaurants helps. Around [37% of Mexican restaurants are quick service](https://datassential.com/resource/mexican-food-growth-united-states/), the preferred format for franchised restaurants. Serving familiar food quickly and cheaply to people on the go is the foundation for many franchises, with cooking treated less as an art form and more as a standardized process, providing wholesome, familiar food wherever customers go. It’s an approach that’s well-suited to standardization and quick setup, and there’s a reason why so many franchisees end up in the quick service sector. Mexican food adapts well to this high-volume style, which has played a part in its spread.

That said, things are currently more challenging than usual for restaurant franchises. The past few years have seen supply chain disruptions and rises in food prices triggered by a number of factors, including the impacts of the Covid pandemic and climate change. As these costs rise, restaurants have to make tough choices about how much of the cost to pass on to customers, many of whom are struggling financially and might be deterred by price rises. Mexican restaurants tend to [operate at a relatively low price point](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/01/11/about-1-in-10-restaurants-in-the-us-serve-mexican-food/), so there’s not a lot of room to soak up the costs.

## Getting Mexican Food Right

A restaurant’s success is very dependent on its location. Quick service restaurants often do well by busy roads or in working districts, where they can sell food to busy people on the move. Foods like tacos that can be easily eaten by hand are particularly good for this.

Other factors also come into play. [The biggest determinant of people’s propensity to dine out is their income level](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/market-research-reports/mexican-restaurants-industry/#IndustryStatisticsAndTrends/), so it’s important when setting up any restaurant to pick a neighborhood with enough wealth to support demand. For Mexican, this might be less about high income customers and more about finding those on a middle income with a bit of cash to spare, who will indulge in taco Tuesday or a Friday night Mexican feast, and who will appreciate an inexpensive dining option.

People there are more likely to be familiar with authentic food and independent eateries, and some may look down on a big chain restaurant run by people with no link to Mexico. An alternative is to look at other regions that are seeing a growth in Mexican restaurants, [such as New York](https://www.npr.org/2024/10/16/nx-s1-5145674/mexican-food-new-york-restaurants-arts), where the spread of Mexican culture has combined with a large population to make a suitable market.

When assessing a franchise, make sure that you understand what its unique selling point is and how that will mesh with your target customer base. Is it providing familiarity and comfort, an exciting new menu, an unusual and exciting Mexican fusion style, or something else?

The Mexican restaurant scene has been growing, and despite economic challenges this looks set to continue. As tacos approach the ubiquity of pizzas and burgers, this is an industry where franchises can play a powerful role.

## The Top Mexican Restaurant Franchises of 2026

### 1. Taco Bell

[Taco Bell](https://www.tacobell.com/franchise) is the reigning champion of Mexican fast food in the US and has been growing rapidly in recent years, opening an average of more than 200 new locations each year during the past decade. While most fast-food places have more or less given up on the dollar menu concept, Taco Bell still has a few items that only cost $1, and several more that are priced at $2. The company has a strong media presence and has had many celebrities in its television commercials, the most recent featuring Pete Davidson.

Founded by Glen Bell in San Bernardino, California, in 1962 and franchising since 1964, the number of locations has continued growing steadily in recent years from 6,053 in 2014 to the current total of 8,746 (up from the previously reported total of 8,565), of which 521 are company-owned and 1,112 are located outside the US.

### 2. Qdoba Mexican Eats

[Qdoba Mexican Eats](https://qdobafranchise.com/) is a fast-casual chain serving up Mexican-style cuisine that includes tacos, taco salads, burritos (San Francisco-style), quesadillas, chili con queso, Mexican gumbo, and many other items. Steak, chicken, and vegetables are fire-grilled in front of customers, pulled pork is roasted daily, and the guacamole is hand-crafted. Customers can top their entrées with guac and queso at no extra charge (first portion only; extra portions are subject to charge).

Founded by Anthony Miller and Robert Hauser in Denver, Colorado, in 1995 and franchising since 1997, the number of locations plateaued for several years but has recently declined to the current total of 691 (up from the previously reported total of 660), of which 167 are company-owned and 17 are located outside the US.

### 3. Del Taco

[Del Taco](https://deltacofranchise.com/) now has a tagline of “Better Mex.” It’s a fusion concept bringing together Mexican and American burgers-and-fries cuisine, though the primary emphasis is the Mex. The menu includes tacos, burritos, epic burritos, quesadillas, nachos, guacamole, crispy chicken, three signature burgers, crinkle cut fries, three kinds of loaded fries, salads, breakfast items, milkshakes, and several dessert options. It emphasizes its quality ingredients, including house-grated cheddar cheese, slow-cooked beans made from scratch, freshly grilled marinated carne asada, freshly grilled marinated chicken, and fresh house-made guacamole.

Founded by Ed Hackbarth in Barstow, California, in 1964 and franchising since 1967, the number of locations currently stands at 588 (down from the previously reported total of 596), of which 116 are company-owned and all are located in the US.

### 4. Moe’s Southwest Grill

[Moe’s Southwest Grill](https://www.moes.com/about/values) presents a menu of Mexican fare, including burritos, quesadillas, nachos, tacos, salads, stacks (quesadilla/taco combination, with the taco wrapped in a grilled tortilla), burrito bowls, and salsas, along with more than 20 different items customers can use to create their own customized meals (every order comes with free chips and salsa). MOE is actually an acronym that stands for “Musicians, Outlaws, and Entertainers,” and the restaurants have a hipster vibe as they play hand-selected music from all kinds of artists and dream up crazy names for menu items with lots of pop culture references.

Founded in 2000 and franchising since 2001, the number of locations had been rising steadily to a peak of 721 in 2018 but has since declined to the current total of 575 (down from the previously reported total of 605), of which five are company-owned and all are located in the US.

### 5. Taco John’s

[Taco John’s](https://tacojohnsfranchise.com/) is a Mexican-inspired fast-food concept it calls “West-Mex.” The menu includes tacos, burritos, quesadillas, and its unique creation, Potato Olés, which are deep-fried seasoned potato nuggets that can be served with or without nacho cheese. Also on the menu are breakfast items, side salads, and several desserts. Taco John’s is the company that trademarked “Taco Tuesday” back in 1989 but recently grew tired of defending it when Taco Bell made the case it’s too common a phrase to be trademarked. Taco John’s relinquished its trademark in July 2023.

Founded by John Turner in Cheyenne, Wyoming, in 1968 and franchising since 1969, the number of locations has been declining in recent years from 393 in 2014 to the current total of 333 (down from the previously reported total of 364), of which seven are company-owned and all are located in the US.

### 6. Quesada Burritos & Tacos

[Quesada Burritos & Tacos](https://quesada.ca/franchising/) is a Canadian chain presenting a Tex-Mex menu of burritos (white or whole wheat tortillas) in three sizes (regular, large, and big ass), burrito bowls, tacos, quesadillas, and a range of sides and add-ons. There are 15 toppings, three salsas, and five sauces. Among the protein toppings for vegetarians is a saucy chipotle tofu. Available meats on the toppings menu are pork al pastor, chile lime fish, flame-grilled chicken, spicy chicken, beef barbacoa, ground beef, and ghost pepper chicken mole.

Founded by Steve Gill in Toronto, Ontario (Canada) in 2003 and franchising since 2010, the number of locations has risen rapidly to the last known reported total of 172 in 2022 (up from the previously reported total of 153), of which two are company-owned and 170 are located outside the US (in Canada).

### 7. Bubbakoo’s Burritos

[Bubbakoo’s Burritos](https://www.bubbakoosfranchise.com/) has a Mexican fusion menu featuring eight signature Killer Burritos or burrito bowls, tacos, a tostada salad, quesadillas, and nachos. These items can also be build-your-own custom ordered. Customers choose their entrée, then choose a protein (nine different meats, vegetarian beans and cheese, or a veggie patty), and finally dress it up with their choices from among 14 different toppings. The menu also allows for several different entrée add-ons, sides, and ten different flavor add-ins (sauces) from mild to crazy-hot (Ghost Pepper). Also on the menu are three Lifestyle Bowls (vegan, vegetarian, keto), chips and dip, hand-tossed wings, curly fries, and several desserts.

Founded by Paul and Bill in Point Pleasant, New Jersey, in 2008 and franchising since 2015, the number of locations has grown rapidly to the current total of 141 (up from the previously reported total of 127), of which 9 are company-owned and all are located in the US.

### 8. On the Border Mexican Grill and Cantina

[On the Border Mexican Grill and Cantina](https://www.ontheborder.com/our-story/franchising/) is a full-service restaurant chain with a large menu consisting of 18 different starters and salads, nine signature fajitas, seven different mesquite grill dishes (mostly quesadillas), 13 Tex-Mex Faves (tacos, burritos, enchiladas, chimichangas), several desserts, a wide array of sides, and hand-crafted alcoholic drinks.

Founded by three friends in Dallas, Texas, in 1982 and franchising since 1996, the number of locations has fallen in recent years from 146 in 2019 to the current total of 134 (down from the previously reported total of 138), of which 109 are company-owned, and 16 are located outside the US.

Founded by three friends in Dallas, Texas, in 1982 and franchising since 1996, the number of locations has fallen in recent years from 146 in 2019 to the last known reported total of 134 in 2022 (down from the previously reported total of 138), of which 109 are company-owned and 16 are located outside the US.

### 9. Fuzzy’s Taco Shop

[Fuzzy’s Taco Shop](https://fuzzystacoshop.com/taco-franchising/) offers up a menu with a dozen different signature Baja Tacos, six different burritos, six burrito bowls, six types of nachos, six signature quesadillas, six different salads, and lots of sides and breakfast items. Franchisees can choose between the traditional standalone location or a smaller Fuzzy’s Taco Shop Taqueria with a smaller footprint, menu, and seating. Unlike most chains, franchisees are free to put some personal touches on their restaurants, within reason and the company’s guidelines.
